authoredSolutions.31: Acetate ion in acetic acid is a weak nucleophile in a polar protic solvent, so the substitution is a solvolysis that goes by \(S_{N}1\) and the rate order is simply the order of carbocation stability. Ionisation of the first chloride gives an allylic cation whose positive charge is delocalised onto the methyl-bearing alkene carbon, i.e. a tertiary allylic cation, the most stable of the four. The second chloride is also allylic but its delocalised cation reaches only secondary centres; the third has chlorine at a non-allylic secondary carbon so no allylic delocalisation is possible; the last is a primary \(CH_{2}Cl\) whose cation gets neither alkyl nor allylic help. The sequence tertiary allylic > secondary allylic > secondary > primary is option (A).
authoredSolutions.32: Adsorption of a gas obeys the Freundlich isotherm \(\frac{x}{m}=kP^{1/n}\) with \(0<\frac{1}{n}<1\), so a plot of \(x/m\) against \(P\) rises steeply at first and then flattens towards saturation. That immediately rules out the two straight-line graphs. Adsorption is exothermic, so raising the temperature shifts the equilibrium back and lowers the amount adsorbed at any given pressure. Since \(T_{1}>T_{2}\), the \(T_{2}\) curve must lie above the \(T_{1}\) curve, and only option (D) shows two saturating curves with \(T_{2}\) on top.
authoredSolutions.33: Portland cement is a mixture of calcium silicates and calcium aluminate obtained by heating limestone with clay. Its approximate composition is tricalcium silicate \(3CaO\cdot SiO_{2}\) about \(51\%\), dicalcium silicate \(2CaO\cdot SiO_{2}\) about \(26\%\) and tricalcium aluminate \(3CaO\cdot Al_{2}O_{3}\) about \(11\%\). The single largest component is therefore tricalcium silicate, option (B).
authoredSolutions.34: The dichromate ion \(Cr_{2}O_{7}^{2-}\) is built from two \(CrO_{4}\) tetrahedra sharing one corner oxygen. Both bridging \(Cr-O\) bonds are of equal length, about \(1.79\) Angstrom, so the bridge is symmetrical. The bridging oxygen still carries lone pairs and uses roughly \(sp^{3}\) orbitals, so the \(Cr-O-Cr\) angle is about \(126^{\circ}\) rather than \(180^{\circ}\). The bridge is therefore non-linear and symmetrical, option (B).
authoredSolutions.35: A \(\beta\)-\(C_{1}-C_{4}\) glycosidic linkage requires the anomeric carbon that forms the link to be in the \(\beta\) configuration. Lactose is galactose joined to glucose through exactly such a \(\beta\)-\(C_{1}-C_{4}\) bond. Maltose and amylose are both built from \(\alpha\)-\(C_{1}-C_{4}\) linkages, and sucrose is joined through \(C_{1}\) of glucose to \(C_{2}\) of fructose, so it is a \(C_{1}-C_{2}\) link. The answer is option (A), lactose.
authoredSolutions.36: The substrate is acetone cyanohydrin, \((CH_{3})_{2}C(OH)CN\), so both branches are transformations of the nitrile group. \(LiAlH_{4}\) followed by aqueous work-up reduces \(-CN\) all the way to a primary amine, so \(A\) is \((CH_{3})_{2}C(OH)CH_{2}NH_{2}\), 1-amino-2-methylpropan-2-ol. With \(H_{3}O^{+}/H_{2}SO_{4}\) the nitrile is hydrolysed and the tertiary alcohol is dehydrated under the strongly acidic conditions, so \(B\) is methacrylic acid, \(CH_{2}=C(CH_{3})COOH\) — this is the industrial acetone-cyanohydrin route to methyl methacrylate. Only option (C) pairs the amino alcohol with methacrylic acid.
authoredSolutions.37: A \(+2\) lanthanide ion is diamagnetic only when it has no unpaired \(4f\) electrons. Ytterbium \((Z=70)\) is \([Xe]4f^{14}6s^{2}\), so losing the two \(6s\) electrons gives \(Yb^{2+}\) with a completely filled \(4f^{14}\) subshell — no unpaired electrons, hence diamagnetic, and the stability of \(f^{14}\) is precisely why \(Yb\) shows the \(+2\) state at all. \(Nd^{2+}\) would be \(4f^{4}\) and \(Ce^{2+}\) \(4f^{2}\), both paramagnetic, while \(La\) has no \(4f\) electrons to stabilise \(+2\). The answer is option (B).
authoredSolutions.38: Aluminium is far too reactive to be reduced by carbon, so purified alumina from bauxite is reduced electrolytically; cryolite \(Na_{3}AlF_{6}\) is added because it lowers the melting point of the charge and greatly increases its electrical conductivity. The assertion is therefore true. In \(Na_{3}AlF_{6}\) the three \(Na^{+}\) and six \(F^{-}\) force aluminium to be \(+3\), so the reason is a true statement as well. However the oxidation state of \(Al\) in cryolite has nothing to do with why cryolite is used, so (R) is not the explanation of (A) — option (D).
authoredSolutions.39: The alcohol shown is 3,3-dimethylbutan-2-ol, \(CH_{3}-CH(OH)-C(CH_{3})_{2}-CH_{3}\). A few drops of concentrated \(H_{2}SO_{4}\) protonate the hydroxyl group; loss of water leaves a secondary carbocation at \(C_{2}\), which relieves its instability by a 1,2-methyl shift from the neighbouring quaternary carbon to give the tertiary cation \((CH_{3})_{2}CH-\overset{+}{C}(CH_{3})_{2}\). Loss of a proton from the adjacent \(CH\) then follows Saytzeff's rule and gives the tetrasubstituted alkene 2,3-dimethylbut-2-ene, the most stable product. That is option (B).
authoredSolutions.40: Novolac is the acid-catalysed phenol-formaldehyde resin. Phenol first adds formaldehyde at the ortho position to give \(o\)-hydroxymethylphenol, and it is this hydroxymethyl derivative that condenses repeatedly to build the linear novolac chain, so it is quoted as the monomer. Phenol with melamine gives melamine-formaldehyde resin, buta-1,3-diene with styrene gives Buna-S, and 3-hydroxybutanoic acid gives PHB. The answer is option (C).
authoredSolutions.41: Statement-I is correct: passing steam over red-hot coke or coal gives a mixture called water gas or synthesis gas, and this process is named coal gasification. Statement-II is wrong, because syn-gas is an equimolar mixture of carbon monoxide and dihydrogen only, \(CO+H_{2}\) in a \(1:1\) ratio; carbon dioxide is not a component of it, appearing only later in the water-gas shift step used to enrich the hydrogen. So Statement-I is true and Statement-II is false, option (B).
authoredSolutions.42: Bromine water adds to propene through a cyclic bromonium ion rather than a free carbocation. The ring carbon that is more substituted bears the greater share of the positive charge, so water attacks there; the hydroxyl group therefore ends up on \(C_{2}\) and bromine on \(C_{1}\), giving 1-bromopropan-2-ol. That is Markovnikov orientation, so the assertion is true, and the Markovnikov opening of the bromonium ion is exactly the reason the observed bromohydrin forms. Both are true and (R) explains (A) — option (C).
authoredSolutions.43: Biuret is \(H_{2}N-CO-NH-CO-NH_{2}\), formed when urea is heated. As a ligand it binds a metal ion (classically \(Cu^{2+}\) in the alkaline biuret test) through two of its nitrogen donor atoms, chelating to form a stable ring. Two donor atoms attached to the same metal centre means it is bidentate, so its denticity is 2 — option (A).
authoredSolutions.44: Across a period the effective nuclear charge rises while the shell stays the same, so electrons are held more tightly: the ionisation enthalpy increases, atoms lose electrons less readily, and metallic character falls while non-metallic character rises. The assertion is therefore true. The reason, however, claims the trend is partly due to a decrease in electron gain enthalpy; in fact the tendency to accept an electron increases across a period (the electron gain enthalpy becomes more negative), so the reason as written is false. Option (B).
authoredSolutions.45: The structure is \(CH_{3}-C(Br)=CH-C\equiv C-CH_{3}\), a six-carbon chain carrying one double and one triple bond. Numbering from the end that gives the unsaturation the lowest locants puts the double bond at \(C_{2}\) and the triple bond at \(C_{4}\), so the parent is hex-2-en-4-yne with bromine on \(C_{2}\). At \(C_{2}\) the bromine outranks the methyl group, and at \(C_{3}\) the alkyne carbon outranks hydrogen; as drawn these two higher-priority groups lie on opposite sides of the double bond, so the configuration is \(E\). The name is (2E)-2-bromo-hex-2-en-4-yne, option (C).
authoredSolutions.46: For an ideal gas \(PV=nRT\). At constant temperature and for a fixed amount of gas the right-hand side is a constant, so the product \(PV\) is completely independent of how the pressure is varied. A plot of \(PV\) against \(P\) is therefore a horizontal straight line parallel to the \(P\) axis, which is option (A). The hyperbola, the line sloping up through the origin and the line sloping down all make \(PV\) depend on \(P\), which is real-gas behaviour, not ideal.
authoredSolutions.47: Simple distillation separates two miscible liquids provided their boiling points differ by roughly \(20^{\circ}C\) or more and they do not form an azeotrope; below that gap the vapour is too rich in both components and fractional distillation is needed instead. Propanone boils at about \(56^{\circ}C\) and propanol at about \(97^{\circ}C\), a difference of some \(41^{\circ}C\), so the mixture can indeed be separated by simple distillation. Both statements are true and the general rule stated in (R) is exactly why (A) works — option (D).
authoredSolutions.48: Depression of freezing point is a colligative property, \(\Delta T_{f}=i\,K_{f}\,m\), so at the same concentration the largest depression belongs to the solute with the largest van't Hoff factor \(i\). Glucose is a non-electrolyte, glycine exists as a neutral zwitterion and hydrazine is only a very weak base, so all three have \(i\) close to \(1\). \(KHSO_{4}\) is a strong electrolyte giving \(K^{+}\) and \(HSO_{4}^{-}\), and the hydrogensulphate ion dissociates further into \(H^{+}\) and \(SO_{4}^{2-}\), pushing \(i\) above \(2\). The largest freezing point depression is therefore option (D).
authoredSolutions.49: Biochemical oxygen demand is the amount of dissolved oxygen micro-organisms need to oxidise the organic matter in a water sample, so it rises directly with the level of organic pollution. Clean water has a BOD below about \(5\) ppm, while heavily polluted water has a BOD above about \(17\) ppm. Only the pair \(A<5\) and \(B>17\) has the clean sample low and the polluted sample high, and every other option makes the clean water the more oxygen-demanding one. The answer is option (C).
authoredSolutions.50: Ethanoic acid with \(SOCl_{2}\) has its \(-OH\) replaced by chlorine, so \(A\) is acetyl chloride \(CH_{3}COCl\). Friedel-Crafts acylation of benzene with this acid chloride and \(AlCl_{3}\) puts the acetyl group on the ring, so \(B\) is acetophenone \(C_{6}H_{5}COCH_{3}\). Cyanide then adds to the ketone carbonyl and the resulting alkoxide is protonated on work-up, so \(C\) is the cyanohydrin \(C_{6}H_{5}C(OH)(CH_{3})CN\), 2-hydroxy-2-phenylpropanenitrile. That structure is option (A).
authoredSolutions.51: Two relations for the same free-energy change give the entropy: \(\Delta G^{\circ}=-nFE_{cell}^{\circ}\) and \(\Delta G^{\circ}=\Delta H^{\circ}-T\Delta S^{\circ}\), so \(\Delta S^{\circ}=\frac{\Delta H^{\circ}+nFE_{cell}^{\circ}}{T}\). Cadmium goes from \(0\) in the metal to \(+2\) in \(CdSO_{4}\), so \(n=2\). Substituting, \(\Delta S^{\circ}=\frac{(-825.2\times10^{3})+(2\times96487\times4.315)}{298}=\frac{-825.2\times10^{3}+832.68\times10^{3}}{298}=\frac{7.48\times10^{3}}{298}\approx 25.1\). To the nearest integer the answer is \(25\).
authoredSolutions.52: The molar mass of oxalic acid dihydrate \(H_{2}C_{2}O_{4}\cdot 2H_{2}O\) is \(2(1)+2(12)+4(16)+2(18)=126\ g\,mol^{-1}\), so \(6.3\ g\) is \(\frac{6.3}{126}=0.05\) mol. Molarity is moles of solute per litre of solution, and \(250\ mL=0.250\ L\), so the concentration is \(\frac{0.05}{0.250}=0.20\ mol\,L^{-1}\). Writing this as \(x\times10^{-2}\) gives \(0.20=20\times10^{-2}\), so \(x=20\).
authoredSolutions.53: In qualitative analysis the group-II sulphides split into a copper sub-group, whose members dissolve in hot \(50\%\ HNO_{3}\), and an arsenic sub-group, which largely resists it. \(PbS\), \(CuS\) and \(CdS\) all dissolve, the nitric acid oxidising sulphide to free sulphur and freeing the metal ion. \(As_{2}S_{3}\) is likewise attacked and taken into solution by the oxidising acid. \(HgS\) is famously inert and needs aqua regia, and \(Sb_{2}S_{3}\) also resists \(50\%\ HNO_{3}\). Four of the six sulphides therefore dissolve, so the answer is \(4\).
authoredSolutions.54: Nitro compounds are reduced to primary amines either by a metal-acid couple or by catalytic hydrogenation. \(Sn-HCl\), \(Fe-HCl\) and \(Zn-HCl\) all supply nascent hydrogen in acid and give aniline (\(Fe-HCl\) being the industrial choice because the \(HCl\) is regenerated), and \(H_{2}\) over \(Pd\) or over Raney nickel reduces the nitro group catalytically. \(Sn-NH_{4}OH\) fails, because a metal-couple reduction needs an acidic medium; in alkaline medium the reduction stops at the coupled products azobenzene, azoxybenzene and hydrazobenzene instead of aniline. Five of the six reagents work.
authoredSolutions.55: A halic(V) acid is an oxoacid of formula \(HXO_{3}\), in which the halogen is in the \(+5\) oxidation state. Chlorine, bromine and iodine all form one: \(HClO_{3}\) chloric acid, \(HBrO_{3}\) bromic acid and \(HIO_{3}\) iodic acid. Fluorine is the most electronegative element and can never take a positive oxidation state, so it forms no oxoacid of this type, and astatine is radioactive and not considered. The number of halogens is \(3\).
authoredSolutions.56: For a first-order reaction \(t=\frac{2.303}{k}\log\frac{a}{a-x}\). At \(50\%\) completion \(\frac{a}{a-x}=2\), so \(t_{50}=\frac{2.303}{k}\log 2\); at \(75\%\) completion \(\frac{a}{a-x}=4\), so \(t_{75}=\frac{2.303}{k}\log 4=\frac{2.303}{k}\times 2\log 2\). Dividing, \(\frac{t_{75}}{t_{50}}=2\) — the same result as noting that \(75\%\) completion is exactly two successive half-lives. The ratio is \(2\).
authoredSolutions.57: In blue vitriol \(CuSO_{4}\cdot 5H_{2}O\) the five water molecules are not equivalent. Four of them are bound directly to \(Cu^{2+}\) as ligands in a square-planar arrangement, giving the \([Cu(H_{2}O)_{4}]^{2+}\) unit. The fifth water is not attached to the metal at all; it sits between the coordinated water molecules and an oxygen of the sulphate ion and is held there only by hydrogen bonds. Hence exactly \(1\) water molecule is hydrogen-bonded.
authoredSolutions.58: In the profile, \(x=20\ kJ\,mol^{-1}\) is measured upward from the \(A+B\) level to the top of the barrier, so it is the forward activation energy \(E_{a,f}\). The \(M+N\) level is reached by dropping \(y=45\ kJ\,mol^{-1}\) below the reactant level, so the barrier seen from the product side is \(E_{a,b}=x+y=65\ kJ\,mol^{-1}\); \(z=15\ kJ\,mol^{-1}\) merely locates the product level above the arbitrary zero of the axis and does not enter the calculation. Therefore \(\Delta H=E_{a,f}-E_{a,b}=20-65=-45\ kJ\,mol^{-1}\), and the required magnitude is \(45\).
authoredSolutions.59: Germanium \((Z=32)\) has the ground-state configuration \(1s^{2}2s^{2}2p^{6}3s^{2}3p^{6}3d^{10}4s^{2}4p^{2}\). Every \(s\) subshell contains exactly one orbital and it has \(m_{l}=0\); every \(p\) subshell contributes one such orbital \((p_{z})\) and every \(d\) subshell one \((d_{z^{2}})\). The ones that are completely filled are \(1s\), \(2s\), \(2p_{z}\), \(3s\), \(3p_{z}\), \(3d_{z^{2}}\) and \(4s\). The two \(4p\) electrons occupy two different \(p\) orbitals singly by Hund's rule, so no \(4p\) orbital is full. Hence \(x=7\).
authoredSolutions.60: The salt dissolves as \(A_{3}B_{2}(s)\rightleftharpoons 3A^{2+}+2B^{3-}\), so if the molar solubility is \(s\) then \([A^{2+}]=3s\) and \([B^{3-}]=2s\). Hence \(K_{sp}=(3s)^{3}(2s)^{2}=27s^{3}\times 4s^{2}=108\,s^{5}\). The solubility is given in \(g\,L^{-1}\), and dividing by the molar mass converts it to \(mol\,L^{-1}\), so \(s=\frac{x}{M}\) and \(K_{sp}=108\left(\frac{x}{M}\right)^{5}\). Comparing with \(K_{sp}=a\left(\frac{x}{M}\right)^{5}\) gives \(a=108\).
authoredSolutions.67: Since \(9x^{2}-12x+4=(3x-2)^{2}\ge 0\), the second factor is \(e^{(3x-2)^{2}}\), which is differentiable everywhere. The first factor \(|(x-3)(x+1)|\) has corners only where it vanishes, at \(x=-1\) and \(x=3\). So \(f\) is not differentiable at exactly two points. Hence (C).
authoredSolutions.71: For the second line, \(q=\frac{|k\sin 2\alpha|}{\sqrt{\sin^{2}\alpha+\cos^{2}\alpha}}=|k\sin 2\alpha|\), so \(q^{2}=k^{2}\sin^{2}2\alpha\). For the first line, \(\csc^{2}\alpha+\sec^{2}\alpha=\frac{4}{\sin^{2}2\alpha}\), hence \(p=\frac{|k\cot 2\alpha|}{2/|\sin 2\alpha|}=\frac{|k\cos 2\alpha|}{2}\) and \(4p^{2}=k^{2}\cos^{2}2\alpha\). Adding, \(4p^{2}+q^{2}=k^{2}\). Hence (A).
authoredSolutions.74: The vertex lies at \((R,0)\) and the focus at \((S,0)\) with \(S>R\), so the vertex-focus distance is \(a=S-R\). The latus rectum has length \(4a=4(S-R)\). Hence (C).
